findings.text: Within the first paragraph a newcomer learns what Athena is, who it is for, and what problem it solves. This covers the 'what is it' and 'why it matters' questions.
findings.source: Header lede: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The page explains why the Athena site opens on a study of a different project (firstmate). Without this, the title "Athena explains how firstmate handles work" would confuse a newcomer about which project the site is about.
findings.source: Header lede: "A study is Athena's written reading of another software project... Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it"

findings.text: A clear next action is linked from the top. Next steps gives prerequisites, the clone and `./setup.sh` commands, and a first command to try (`athena ask "add a changelog"`), so the reader knows what to do next.
findings.source: Header: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" and the Next steps section

findings.text: The page says Athena is written in Rust but does not list a Rust toolchain as a prerequisite. A newcomer can't tell whether `setup.sh` installs Rust or whether they need it already. This is my inference from the page; I did not check setup.sh.
findings.source: Next steps: "have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm"

findings.text: This link is for the repository owner, but it sits next to the newcomer's next step without saying who it is for. A first-time visitor may think there are decisions waiting for them.
findings.source: Header: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: Most of the page is a dense state-machine description of firstmate with claim ids on every line. It shows how rigorous Athena is, but someone who came to learn about Athena will likely skim it. Only the three header paragraphs and Next steps speak to them directly.
findings.source: Sections "States of a piece of work", "Counters", "Transitions" (t1–t12)

findings.text: The "Start here" section and "Words used first" make the firstmate material approachable. Terms like captain, yolo, green and red are defined before they are used, and the walkthrough of one piece of work is easy to follow.
findings.source: Start here: "The three parts below say what firstmate is, follow one piece of work, and say what happens when something fails"

findings.text: The page says plainly what its sources don't support, here and in "Limits of this study" ("none was run"). That builds trust in the traceability promise from the header.
findings.source: Words used first, "in scope": "The cited instruction does not say what makes work in scope, so this page gives no test for it."
